analysis.one_liner: Freezes evictions, foreclosures, and most rent increases for a year, while sending federal loans and grants to renters, homeowners, and landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee, ending with zero cosponsors when the Congress expired in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This pandemic housing bill would have banned evictions and foreclosures for one year, frozen rent increases to the rate of inflation, and given tenants 18 months to repay missed rent. It would have expanded mortgage forbearance, blocked landlords and lenders from reporting missed payments to credit agencies, sent $20 billion to help low-income households keep the lights and water on, and given landlords low-cost federal loans and grants to cover lost rent. It also added bankruptcy protections for people who lost income because of COVID-19.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who could not pay rent would have been protected from eviction for a year, would not have faced rent hikes, would have had 18 months to catch up, and would not have had the missed payments or an eviction show up on their credit record. Homeowners would have gotten automatic forbearance, no penalty fees, and a mandatory loan-modification offer before any foreclosure. Low-income households would have gotten help paying energy and water bills, with shutoffs banned. People in bankruptcy would have kept COVID aid out of creditors' reach and gotten a much larger homestead exemption. Small landlords would have gotten federal grants and low-cost loans, on condition they did not evict.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, struggling homeowners, and small landlords

how_it_helps.text: Bans evictions and foreclosures for one year, freezes rent increases to the rate of inflation, and gives tenants 18 months to repay missed rent without late fees.

Bars landlords and mortgage servicers from reporting missed rent, evictions, or missed mortgage payments to credit bureaus during the pandemic period, protecting tenants' and homeowners' credit scores.

Expands mortgage relief beyond the CARES Act: borrowers who fell 60 days behind get automatic forbearance, servicers cannot charge fees or penalty interest, and a servicer must offer a loan modification that does not raise the monthly payment before starting foreclosure.
Authorizes $20 billion in grants to states and tribes to pay overdue energy and water bills for low-income households, on condition utilities keep service connected and waive pandemic-era late fees.
Provides $1.2 billion for housing legal aid and counseling targeted to low-income and minority households, plus grants to states guaranteeing tenants facing illegal eviction a right to an attorney.

Helps landlords absorb the cost of the moratorium through a Federal Reserve credit facility offering long-term, low-cost loans and a $1 billion grant program for owners of 10 or fewer properties — both conditioned on not evicting tenants for nonpayment.

Adds bankruptcy protections: federal COVID aid is excluded from bankruptcy estates, the federal homestead exemption rises from $15,000 to $100,000, and homeowners get up to 7 years to cure mortgage defaults in Chapter 13.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords would bear deferred rent (not forgiven) and a year without rent increases or evictions for nonpayment, though federal loans and grants would offset much of the loss. Mortgage investors and servicers would absorb forbearance costs, escrow advances, and mandatory loss-mitigation offers, in exchange for a legal shield from investor lawsuits. Utilities would have to waive pandemic-era late fees and keep service connected, though federal grants would pay most arrears. Taxpayers would fund the credit facility, the $20 billion utility program, and the legal-aid, counseling, and grant programs — over $21 billion in authorized appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords, mortgage investors, utilities, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Missed rent is deferred, not forgiven: tenants could leave the moratorium owing up to 18 months of back rent, and the 18-month repayment schedule could still be unaffordable for households whose incomes never recovered.

The bill routes landlord compensation through a Federal Reserve credit facility open to any rental property owner; the only check on large corporate landlords is a report to Congress identifying who owns more than 1,000 units, plus a ban on using relief funds to buy distressed properties.

It gives mortgage servicers a broad safe harbor from investor lawsuits and guarantees them access to federal liquidity — protections the industry sought — in exchange for complying with the forbearance rules.

It quietly extends the GSE patch, a rule that lets lenders issue mortgages above the normal ability-to-repay standards, until June 2022 — a loosening of lending standards unrelated to pandemic relief.

A year-long freeze on rent increases and evictions, with costs deferred to landlords, could lead some owners to sell, convert units, or skimp on maintenance — a cost honest supporters would have to weigh against keeping families housed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households the moratorium would have kept housed, the benefits were large and immediate — no eviction, no foreclosure, no credit wreckage during a jobs collapse. The design costs are real but mostly shifted rather than avoided: rent deferred is not rent erased, so the deepest problem (households owing more than they can ever repay) is pushed to the end of the 18-month window, and much of the burden on landlords and servicers is offset by federal money, meaning taxpayers ultimately share the bill. The servicer safe harbor and the GSE patch extension are giveaways folded into an otherwise consumer-focused bill. On balance it is a strong bill for ordinary people with some costly loose ends.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kamala Harris introduced the RELIEF Act on August 10, 2020, about five months into the pandemic's economic shutdown.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the standard first step for a housing bill.
No other action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate. The bill listed zero cosponsors.
When the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, the bill died with it; a bill not passed by both chambers is gone for good and would have to start over in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, mortgage servicers, and credit bureaus benefited because none of the new rules — the year-long eviction and foreclosure ban, the rent freeze, the credit-reporting prohibition, the mandatory loss-mitigation offers — ever took effect. Renters and homeowners got nothing from this bill, though other federal and state relief existed separately.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the chamber never debated or voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no voting record exists; the only sign of support was one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-run Senate never considered the bill.

industries.note: They would lose a year of evictions for nonpayment and face a rent-inflation-only freeze, but the bill pays them back with a Fed credit facility, CARES Act liquidity, and $1 billion in small-owner grants — and they could still collect the deferred rent from tenants over 18 months. Their gain from blocking the bill was avoiding those constraints entirely.

Servicers would have to grant automatic forbearance, advance escrow payments, and offer loan modifications before foreclosure, but in exchange they get a safe harbor from investor lawsuits, guaranteed access to federal liquidity programs, and 12 months after forbearance to bring loans current without fees.

Forbearance without fees or penalty interest, deferrals, and modification offers would come out of investor cash flows; the bill responds by declaring forbearance standard industry practice and shielding servicers from investor claims.

industries.industry: Consumer reporting and tenant screening agencies
industries.note: The bill bans reporting of pandemic-era evictions, unpaid rent, and missed mortgage payments, cutting off a stream of data — including eviction records that follow tenants for years — that these firms sell to landlords.

They would have to waive pandemic-era late fees and keep service connected to homes in arrears, but $20 billion in federal grants would pay most household arrears and reconnection fees directly to the system.

industries.industry: Private equity and distressed real estate investors
industries.note: The bill bars any business entity except nonprofits and mission-focused affordable housing developers from using federal relief funds to buy distressed mortgages, foreclosed homes, or real-estate-owned properties — closing a channel through which well-capitalized firms typically acquire housing in a downturn.
